It seems to me there is a great gap in the present practice when the department does not require the filing by the contractor of a performance bond by some surety company. That is very general practice in private life with large construction contracts. I think it would be of very great value to the department itself as well as to those who are subcontractors of those who are contractors of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is something in that argument of the performance bond. I understand that it was studied by those in this line of business, but in the past those bonds have always been refused. We do not accept them; we ask for a cash deposit of 10 per cent of the amount of the contract or tender from the companies that tender.
I understand that this question of a bond is being studied. I would not see any serious objection, but I do not think the protection would be greater for the government than the cash security deposit. Take this instance where unfortunately the man did not complete the contract. We had the money to go ahead, and we did if. In the contract in question, if we did lack some money to complete it we would have our recourse against

the contractor for the balance. That would be all right if he were solvent. If he were bankrupt we would lose, probably, but we do not lose very much money in our contracts. I may tell the hon. member that there are not many cases where we lose money.
Will the hon. member for Eglin-ton tell us how a performance bond would be helpful to the Lunam contractors under these circumstances?

In view of the term in the contract about which I asked the minister a question when I rose to my feet. If it were not a provision in the contract the department has with the contractor that the contractor engages to pay his subcontractors and thereby incurs an obligation to the minister to pay them, then the performance bond would be of doubtful value as far as subcontractors are concerned. Even then it would be of value to the department, but in view of the fact that there is a provision in the contract that the contractor undertakes as an obligation to the minister to pay his subcontractors, then the performance bond would be of very definite value. That prompts me to ask another question of the minister.
Would you get a performance bond under these conditions?

Yes, I think you would; and I think this, and I speak from some experience in such matters. I think it would be of very definite value also in eliminating people who are tendering who are not potentially solvent. You would not find surety companies agreeing to give performance bonds to people who are not solvent, and I think it would represent another measure of guarantee against a situation of this kind arising in the future.
There is one other aspect to this subject that I should like to raise. I think the minister can see that the materialman who is supplying material to a contractor with his department is not in the same position as a materialman who is supplying material to a contractor on private property. He is denied the normal benefits that flow to the subcontractor, the materialman and the wage earner under the mechanics' lien act. In these circumstances it seems to me that in all fairness something more is required on the part of the department than just to say, "We will take no responsibility. We will just treat this as we would if the structure were being built on private property".
It may be all very well for the owner in a case of that kind, where the land is privately owned, to say, "Well, you materialmen, you must protect yourselves. You have the mechanics' lien act." This is a different situa-

tion and, Mr. Chairman, it is quite evident that whatever may be said for the 10 per cent deposit or the 10 per cent holdback as a measure of guarantee to the department, we have abundant evidence in this case that it has left a great gap in the security extended to those who ought to have some consideration from the department by reason of the fact that they are denied the normal protection of the mechanics' lien act of the province.
There is one further matter about which I should like to question the minister. In view of the terms of the contract which he mentioned in reply to my first question, it is evident that, even though there was sufficient in the deposit and the holdback to enable the department to complete the building in this case, there still has been a breach of contract on the part of the contractor if he has broken that provision of his contract under which he obligated himself to pay to the materialmen and the wage earners the money due them. What action, if any, has the Department of Public Works taken with reference to that breach of contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are trying to complete these three buildings. That is the first thing I had in mind, to see if we had enough money. We probably will not be through with this gentleman when we have completed the job. We will know exactly where we stand then. We shall assure ourselves whether or not he is really solvent.
Did I understand the minister to say that the buildings were not completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Two out of the three are completed and the other is being completed, and I have given the hon. member for Lake Centre the amount necessary to complete it. This is the way this case strikes me as a lawyer. Here is a man who stopped doing the work some time ago, sometime in January, as I explained.
In what year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In 1952. We received no claim from anybody before that. He had stopped doing the work for I do not know how long, two or three or four months, and then we started getting claims. Now, even if these people were entitled to collect under the mechanics' lien statute the time for registering "their liens would have expired by that time.
They cannot file a mechanic's lien against the crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I know, but even if they had the right against the government the time had expired. The man stops work, and they wait for two or three months before we hear of a claim. Even if they were entitled
Supply-Public Works
to all the benefits under that statute, their delay in putting in their claims would have barred them.
Not if the building was not completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If the delivery had been made before.
No, not in British Columbia, at any rate. It may be that way in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not going to go into that, although it is interesting as a legal point. All this discussion should prove one thing. Even if you can blame my officials in certain instances, they try to get the work done according to the contract and the amount of money we have asked from parliament. I think I have to give them credit for that. They are not perfect; they may have defects, but they are quite loyal and frank with me, and I think I know almost everything-well, I would not say everything-that goes on in my department. When they have difficulties they bring them to my attention. Here is one of the difficulties they had. I was acquainted with it, and that was the procedure we followed.

It occurs to me that something depends upon what was said in that affidavit. Has the minister gone carefully into the affidavit that was taken? If so, is there anything wrong with it, or is it exactly in accordance with the facts?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My deputy tells me it is the ordinary form of affidavit that is mentioned in the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. Personally I do not see them, but that is the information I have.

I seems to me there is a real problem involved here, if the affidavit is contrary to the facts which obtained at the time it was taken. Some responsibility rests with the government as to what steps it will take.
One further question-
No, I should like to have the minister give me that information, because it is important.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have not looked
into that aspect of the matter. What I had in mind when this matter was brought to my attention was to have completion of the buildings with the money we had on hand. At the time I did not even know there were claims coming in. I said, "Now, get the estimate, and see what we can do with that money." The report came back that we could complete the three buildings with the money we had from the security deposit and

Supply-Public Works
the holdback from payments. That was the practical thing I had in mind. This afternoon I have given the result. As to the other point, well, I must confess ignorance. I have not given much thought to it.
At some other stage will the minister give the information I have asked for? I think it is of much more importance than appears on the surface.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will; but at this stage I would not know the decision of the department as to what proceedings we would take against the man. I would not go that far. I would have to consult the Department of Justice. We would bring it to their attention and they would advise us as to the procedure to be followed, if any.
The minister does not have any objection to giving us a copy of the affidavit sworn by the contractor, has he?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shall look into it.

I have been listening to the discussion, and I wonder if I am right in my belief that during that discussion someone said there were no judgments against this man as a result of the debts owing. Am I correct in that understanding? When he was discussing the matter the hon. member for Lake Centre did not indicate that there were any judgments, and from what the minister said I gathered there were no judgments. Am I correct?

I cannot answer for the minister, but my information is that the only asset this company had was a house owned by Lunam at the time he ceased work, and that he transferred that house to his wife. So I think the assets were pretty well cleared away. But that does raise a question I should like to ask the minister. He was able to advise the house, on the basis of an article in a Regina newspaper, that Mr. Lunam was not bankrupt. In that article Mr. Lunam said he was not bankrupt.
In view of the fact that claims from suppliers approximating $170,000 have been sent to the department-and the information I have as to the amount still owing suppliers *came in an answer furnished by the minister in the house-has the minister been in touch with the Lunam Construction Company to find out what assets they have, and whether they will make payments? That would appear to be a most salutary course to follow, rather than to ascertain through the medium of a press interview that Mr. Lunam was not bankrupt. And if the minister has been in communication with the Lunam Construction Company, will he place before the committee balance sheets showing, among other

things, the indebtedness of the Lunam Construction Company, and to whom. If the minister has that statement we would like to have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Replying to the first
question, the hon. member has said that the only asset Lunam had was a house. He will understand that Lunam tendered on contracts amounting to $1,200,000. One sure thing is that we held back 10 per cent, which would have amounted to $100,000. We must have had that much from him. I do not know where he got it, but he must have had some assets or he would not have got those contracts just by attaching his cheque to the tender. We never ask more than a 10 per cent deposit from any people tendering on these contracts. He met that requirement. Since he has been out of the hospital I am told he cannot be found. If the hon. member could help me find him I would be very glad indeed. I do not know where he is, but we have inquired.
I do not think he could have been looked for very thoroughly, because he was in Regina six weeks ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, I did not go
personally to Regina to look for him, but I did ask some in the department, and they tried to locate him. We went to a hotel where he had been living at one time, but he had moved out of that hotel and gone to another one. We tried to locate him there. The first news I got was this clipping from the newspaper. I do not know where he is.

Well, he gave that
interview in Regina.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, but it may have been given on the street corner, and when I would get out there he would be on the next corner. We are still trying to find him.

So is it a fact that since February, 1952, the Department of Public Works has not been in communication with Mr. Lunam, or secured from him a balance sheet showing his assets and liabilities? Has he just disappeared, faded away, only to be found by a reporter of the Regina Leader-Post for an interview?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Here is the information my officials give me on this case, that since February 1952 we have tried to locate the man and have not succeeded. So we have had no contact with him, no balance sheet or anything else. And as we wanted to complete the buildings, we got to work on them.

Are all
these contracts by the Department of Public Works on an outright basis? Are they all

outright contracts, or does the department on some occasions pay a fixed fee, or cost plus? Does the department make contracts on a cost-plus basis? I remember that the Auditor General told the public accounts committee that on some occasions a person will have a contract with the government on which further work to be done is carried out on a cost-plus basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If my hon. friend
wishes to have that information I would advise him to read section 36 of the Public Works Act. If he will read it carefully he will see how these contracts are given. It is all written down in black and white.

If the
minister knows what is in section 36, would he be good enough to tell me now?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is one section
which authorizes me, when it is in the public interest, to give contracts in amounts up to $15,000 without asking for tenders. Over and above the amount, in urgent cases, where damage would occur to the public interest if I were to fail to take action, I can make contracts without tenders. Outside of that we must ask for tenders.
When you come to make payments on those contracts, do you not have affidavits covering materials used? Those would have been paid for before you pay for the contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have been arguing that for two hours.

I am anxious to see this item pass, but I think it would be wrong to allow the impression to continue which has been created on the minister this afternoon without endeavouring to set out both sides of the picture. I think we should analyse just how this situation arose. Anyone familiar with the conditions surrounding a contract of this kind knows that the local firms who are supplying goods to the general contractor are not anxious to have payments made at the end of the month for fear they might lose some future business. In other words they deliberately get themselves into the position where the general contractor owes them large sums of money. They partly finance his contract so they will continue to get his business.' That is a position into which they get of their own volition.
Having explained how the situation arose and why they are in that position, I would not want the minister to gum up the procedure with red tape by putting into effect any of the suggestions that have been made by the opposition lawyers. If you are going to require the inspector to have receipts for
Supply-Public Works
all bills that are paid, you will also need to have an engineer, an auditor and a chartered accountant. Then if the department happened to pay one of these bills and through fraud were asked to pay it a second time you would immediately be held responsible for having made that mistake.
I hope that you will not start to further gum up with red tape these contracts that have been discussed today by following the procedure that has been suggested by the opposition.
Did the minister at any time secure from the Lunam Construction Company a statement of assets and liabilities? Did he ever ask for such a statement before or after February, 1952.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: To which contracts would that question apply?
Just the ones under public works.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Those that were completed and paid for. We have those buildings. Should I get a statement on those? In the case of those that are not completed, I have the money to complete them.
That does not answer anything. I do not know why the minister has not done something regarding this matter. He has the mounted police available.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I object to that, and I want my hon. friend to withdraw his statement. I have been talking here this afternoon for nearly two hours telling what I have been doing. I do not think it is fair that the hon. member should say I have not been doing anything. I would not say that to the hon. gentleman, although I do not believe he is doing very much.
To say that the minister has not been doing anything is possibly an understatement, because what I had in mind was this. This man disappeared in Regina.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: How do you know he is in Regina?
Everybody knew, including the staff reporter of the Regina Leader-Post who interviewed this man on several occasions.

How
did he know him?

I am not going to answer that. Presumably his identity was made known to him. On the statement that was secured I cannot understand why the Department of Public Works, having actually benefited to the extent of approximately $170,000

Supply-Public Works
worth of materials that went into the buildings so they could be completed within the contract price, did not do anything. In other words, if the suppliers had not been taken in to the extent of $170,000 in materials that were supplied, as far as the government is concerned the projects would have cost much more to complete over and above the contract price.
Has the minister's department written to the Lunam company? If they have, I should like to have the correspondence produced' when we come to the proper item. This man's elusiveness was such that it aroused great interest. Lunam and his company took these people in to the extent they did as the result of a false affidavit, and only the Department of Public Works can prosecute because the false pretence was perpetrated against that department. This man swore a false affidavit which caused the Department of Public Works to advance moneys to which he was not entitled, and I cannot understand why he should not have been prosecuted or why the mounted police were not used to ascertain whether a fraud such as this should be committed against the Department of Public Works.
That is the reason I said the minister had not done anything. I meant that he had not used the agencies that were available in order to punish a man who according to the statement of the minister is a wrongdoer in that he defrauded the government of Canada by falsely swearing to an affidavit in order to secure payment. I am wondering whether the matter was ever placed in the hands of the mounted police, or whether there were communications with Lunam or the company?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
After this accident
had happened and he was in the hospital, and we found out he could not proceed with the construction, we had served on him a notice according to the contract that we would hold as security the balance of the contract and would proceed with the work. I understand that we have a copy of that contract.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Architectural branch-[DOT]
322.	Ottawa-maintenance and operation of public buildings and grounds, including repairs and upkeep, rents, furnishings, heating, etc., and to authorize commitments against future years in the amount of $500,000, $13,588,361.
Will the minister tell the committee to what extent commitments are authorized against future years? Apparently each year there is a provision of this type in this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This $500,000 for
future commitments covers orders which are given during the fiscal year but which are not expected to be delivered. Suppose we ordered a diesel engine which takes many months to deliver, we would be committed to the company but would not receive delivery during the fiscal year. We have to have this amount for future commitments.
To what extent?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am told that this
year we are committed to the extent of about $300,000. These goods will be delivered in the future, but not under this vote. If we did not have this item we would have no legal power to give an order.
These commitments were made in the last fiscal year and are for the present fiscal year; is that the idea?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

Why is there a provision of
this kind in this and the following item, and not in any other item?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am told that in the
last months of the fiscal year we continue placing orders although we know they will not be delivered. We are authorized to commit up to $500,000 under this item for the next year, but these amounts will be revoted as deliveries are made in the next year. It is only authority to commit; it is not an expenditure of money. We cannot go over and above our commitments for $500,000. I understand that in the administration, when the last months of the year come we have to continue to give notice of what we need. We say well, let us place the order and in the next estimates we will ask for the amount. If we did not have that authority we would have to stop ordering for delivery in the new fiscal year.
Why is it necessary for these items and not for any other items?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
These are the two
maintenance items in my department. The other items are specific items for contractual purposes; but these are the two items which cover maintenance of all buildings in the country.

There is quite a large increase in some of the amounts under this item. I am looking at page 393. There, for example, we find a big increase in furniture and furnishings for government departments. The increase there is about $60,000, and it was also increased last year over the year 1951-52. Rents also are increased by $550,000. Light, power, water, etc. are increased by about $70,000. These are all expenditures

to be made in Ottawa. Why is there that large increase for the present fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is an increase this year of $725,622.
I am asking about item 322 and the minister has given the wrong figure. He has given the figure for outside Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is an increase in salaries from $4,250,715 to $4,566,083. That would comprise increases in salaries that have been granted during the year plus the addition probably of a few salaries and wages, due principally to increases in prevailing rates of pay, statutory increases, and an increase of 90 in the char staff to take care of the new buildings. There is $315,000 in that.
There is an increase of $62,500 in the allotment for furniture and furnishings for government departments, due mainly to special provision being made in the vote for the first time for upholstering and repairs to furniture, and acquisition of Venetian blinds. There is an increase in rents because we have taken over four more buildings in Ottawa, the Ogilvy building, the Metcalfe building, 245 Sparks street, and the seminary building. There is an increase of $75,640 for light, power and water covering new buildings and rented premises, provision for unemployment insurance contributions and so forth. There is a decrease in the allotments for travelling expenses, materials and supplies, moving government departments, and taxes on diplomatic properties, in the amount of $208,000. That leaves a net increase of $830,943.
May I ask the minister whether it is under this item that provision is made for maintenance and upkeep of the Prime Minister's residence?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A total of $10,950 was provided in the summary for the Prime Minister's residence. The vote for 1953-54 for the Prime Minister's residence is as follows:	Payment to steward as representative of this department in the household, $1,000; furnishing, $4,000; fuel for residence and coach house, $1,750; repairs, painting, etc., $3,400; electric power, $800.
Does that include all the expenses, operating expenses as well as upkeep of the building? I understand that the operating expenses also fall within this department.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is certainly what it costs my department.

Where are the operating expenses charged?
Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Do hon. gentlemen not think I have enough? I am giving what it costs me.
What department is responsible?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
What department
spends more money? I do not know if there are any other departments, and I do not know which one if any. I know what I spend, and this is the amount.
According to the statute that was passed several years ago, the maintenance of this property as well as the operating expenses of the residence all come under this department.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Read the section again. You will see that is not correct. Maintenance is what I am paying here.
Are we to understand that operating expenses of the residence do not fall within the Department of Public Works?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If that is so I have
not been operating it.

In the five items given by
the minister, totalling some $10,000, there is an amount of $3,400 indicated for repairs this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Right.
What justifies such a high figure for repairs on a building that was completed only two years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This is only an
estimate and it has not been spent. You have not given it to me yet.

I quite realize that, but
what repairs are contemplated which would justify the minister asking for $3,400 for repairs to a building that was completed only about two years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told there will be some repainting outside the building and some work inside the building. With respect to the details of how many windows and how many doors need repair I have not the information. You want us to maintain the residence in a good state so a man was sent down to look over the building, and he reported we would need about $3,400 in the year to do that work.
How much was expended on repairs in the fiscal year just ended?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have not that
information.

Well, I think that information should be available. I quite understand that the minister might not have it for the full twelve months-

Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will get it.
-but he should have it complete for eleven months and might perhaps estimate for the twelfth month.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have not the figures here, but I will get them.
When can we have them?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As soon as I have a moment.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall the item
carry?

No. The minister explained
that there had been several new buildings rented in Ottawa during the year. I did not hear what they were, and I wonder if he would give them again and tell us in each case what the rent is and what the building is used for.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The main new buildings rented are the Ogilvy building, the Metcalfe building, 245 Sparks street, and the seminary building. Those are the four that were rented in this last fiscal year and account for increasing the amount.

What are the rents in each
case, and for what purposes are those buildings used?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Do you want me to
read the list of all the rents for the buildings in Ottawa?
No, just those four.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The total is $550,000
per year. I have a list of all the buildings we occupy.
I only want the rentals for those four buildings, and the purposes for which the buildings are used.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Metcalfe building is used for national defence and the rental is $76,610; the Ogilvy building, national defence, and the rental is $61,922; the seminary rental is $370,000; 245 Sparks street is for defence production and labour, rented from the Bank of Canada, $48,000.

For what purpose is the
seminary used?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The whole of the
mounted police organization has been transferred to that building from the justice building and the six or seven other buildings in which they occupied space.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
323.	Maintenance and operation of public buildings and grounds, other than at Ottawa, including repairs and upkeep, rents, furnishings, heating, etc., and to authorize commitments against future years in the amount of $800,000, $18,998,865.

Does this item include the
maintenance of Canada House in St. John's, Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, we do not maintain it. I understand we receive a rental from the province of $1,500 per year.
You say you do not maintain it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

May I read an answer to a question which appears in Hansard for March 16, page 2958. The question was:
What is the annual cost of maintenance of this property?
The answer was:
Fiscal year 1949-50; $281.76; fiscal year 1950-51, $34.80; fiscal year 1951-52, $118.17.
I do not know who is paying it. Is that your department?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
When I said no, I
asked my officials whether we maintained the place. We cannot do much maintenance for $34.80 in a year. The answer must have been prepared by somebody in the department who had more knowledge than I have or the gentlemen I have here with me. My impression is that we have no maintenance costs, but we do get a rental from the province of Newfoundland.

Well, those figures were just in error, I take it. May I ask another question to which the minister may be able to give a reply now that he has his senior officials with him. On that same page of Hansard I asked whether the property was owned by Canada, and the answer was yes. Then I asked:
If so, when was it purchased?
The answer was:
It was taken over when Newfoundland entered confederation.
That does not mean anything to me. Will the minister explain what that means?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If the hon. member
reads the terms of union he will find that part of the buildings that were serving government purposes in Newfoundland were transferred to the central government. Probably this would be one of the buildings that fell to our lot. I may say that public works has taken over more than one building. That is to the best of my recollection. The hon. member has on the order paper another question concerning that matter. I was told today that external affairs were handling that answer, so I just forgot about it.

Is this not the position? The property known as Canada House had been

bought by Canada before Newfoundland came into confederation and was owned by Canada at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My officials say you are probably right.
I am probably right? The minister knows I am right. What is the meaning of this phrase, then, that it was taken over?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: To make it clear, I am told that before union, external affairs had purchased that building from the commission of government, and since-
No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, you know the story.

Let me give you the facts. The property was purchased from a private individual. I do not know what department purchased it but I am assuming it was your department. The building was used to house the high commissioner, and at the time of the consummation of union it was rented to the government of Newfoundland. I want to find out the purchase price of the building when it was originally bought.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would not have that information. It was purchased by external affairs to house the high commissioner for Canada in Newfoundland.
You mean there is no chance of finding out at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, when the external affairs officials are before the committee. You have that committee on external affairs, and you can find out there.
Is this not the proper place to ask about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, it was transferred to public works. I did not make an inspection to find out if it was paid for by cash or with a note. We took it over, and we rented it to the province later on.
I shall not plague the minister, then, because he has been plagued enough today. Would he be prepared to give a full answer on this tomorrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told that you could see in the public accounts for 1946-47, when it was purchased.
The other matter the minister is going to look up is how I got these figures for maintenance.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will get that information.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Supply-Public Works
Acquisition, construction and improvements of public buildings-
Construction, acquisition, major repairs and improvements of, and plans and ^ sites for, public buildings listed in the details of the estimates, provided that treasury board may increase or decrease the amount within^ the vote to be expended on individual listed projects-
324.	Newfoundland, $550,000.

This is the place where the minister asked me to raise the question about revotes. For instance, on page 396 I find that out of nine items listed for item 324 amounting to $550,000, actually there are revotes totalling more than $550,000. There is an allowance of some $67,000 made for overestimates or amounts that will not be spent. I just cannot understand how a government of experts last year asked for $575,000 of which they did not spend one cent. There are seven items for _ which money was voted a year ago, of which not a dollar was spent. It would appear that seven of those items are entire revotes. The minister explained that you get a certain amount of money and you are not able to finish a building so you have a revote, but here is a case where the whole amount is revoted. I would like some explanation of that, because I am going to bring up the matter in connection with the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Let us take the first item, Bishop's Falls public building. To complete this there will be a revote of $45,000. You understand that in this case the work is under contract and it is proceeding. We expect to complete the work and we need a further amount of $62,000 for this fiscal year, which comprises an amount of $45,000 which was voted to us last year and which I am asking the house to revote this year.
Now take the second case, in which there is a revote for the Clarenville public building. This amount is to provide for the purchase of a site and the erection of a public building to accommodate the post office and customs at Clarenville. The proposed building is strongly requested by the customs division, who state they are now located in a very dilapidated building which is entirely unsuitable. The Post Office Department has also requested space in the proposed building. Pending preparation of preliminary plans the total cost is tentatively estimated at $75,000. This was voted last year. I do not think we have succeeded as yet in purchasing the site. We hope to purchase a site. When we get the site we will have the officials in the department prepare plans. We expect that during this fiscal year we may be able to spend part of that $75,000.

Supply-Public Works
What about the other items? They are all the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I could read the
whole book and you would get about the same explanation as this. Here is one. It is at Corner Brook. A site satisfactory to the Post Office Department as to location and to the chief architect as to size has been selected. This site located on Main street is owned by Bowater's (Newfoundland) Pulp and Paper Mills and has been offered for sale at a price of $18,000. This area involves approximately 36,000 square feet. As the asking price is considered fair and reasonable, negotiations are being undertaken to acquire the site. If we purchase that site during this year, we will have plans prepared; and if they are ready during the fiscal year we will ask for tenders and give out the contract. What we will be able to spend on this I cannot tell.
Mr. Nose worthy: What is the explanation of the fact that each year your experts estimate how much of that estimated expenditure will remain unspent In the case of Newfoundland last year they estimated that they would probably ask for $137,000 more than would be spent. Actually they asked for $575,000 more than was spent. That situation applies all the way through the architectural branch of this department. In Nova Scotia you find four items which were not touched at all. Nova Scotia had a fairly good record there.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Shall we pass this
first item? Then when we reach Nova Scotia I will give more information.
All right; take them one at a time.

May I ask
the minister whether anything has been done about the two buildings there for which provision is made, namely the public building
and the customs building?
In St. John's.
Yes, in St. J ohn's.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This amount is required' to purchase a site and for preparation of plans and specifications for a proposed building at St. John's, Newfoundland, to provide improved accommodation for the customs services. It is now proposed to erect the new building on the site of the existing building which will be enlarged by the acquisition of property between the site and the war memorial square. The additional property to be acquired consists of four parcels of land, and there are three owners 
involved. Valuations of the property were prepared for the department by H. J. Thomas and Son, St. John's, and by Willett Engineering and Surveying Company, St. John's. I do not know whether I should give these figures. I would rather keep these valuations undisclosed until we negotiate. But I have valuations for the whole of the property and we are negotiating with these people for the purchase of the properties. I think hon. members should not insist that I give those amounts.

I do not
insist on the disclosure of that information.
What is the building supposed to be for? What is the general idea?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is for the
customs.
To what size do you propose to enlarge it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I know that the estimated cost will be in the neighbourhood of $550,000.

That is not very big. Is
that the cost of the building alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the estimated cost.

The total
cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We will know more
about it when the plans are prepared and when we are owners of the site.
I suppose the plans are prepared now before you have bought that land?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is rather difficult, before we become owners of the site, to prepare final plans. We have to make those plans conform to the site on which the building will be erected.
Is it proposed to begin construction shortly?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As soon as I can purchase the site we will start working on it. The other case I would say we will let stand. I have not purchased the site and, judging by the clippings that were read in the house, it seems that I am having difficulty in getting the proper site for that building.
Is it fair to assume that you are not going to put it on government house ground?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Do not ask me that.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Because I could not give you an answer.
The last time you were talking to me here in the chamber you told me that all that remained was the purchase price to be negotiated between you and the premier of Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have not reached that stage.
Have you changed your mind since?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have not reached that stage yet.
Of changing your mind?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would not answer that question.

May I ask
the minister whether any progress has been made in respect of the other two, St. Lawrence and Stephenville. They are revotes here of the full amounts.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have not got the sites. Here is the estimated cost of $55,000. For the site we expect to pay about $5,000, for the building, $45,000; for supervision and contingencies, $5,000. The other one is for Stephenville. The site selected for this building adjoins the existing post office building and measures 100 feet along the highway to Kippens and 100 feet along the highway to Stephenville Crossing. The owner has offered to sell the property for the sum of $2,500.
The only question I really want to ask is this. Is there a good chance of the work going ahead this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is why we have the estimate. We live in hope that during the fiscal year it will be possible.

May I revert to the public building in St. John's for one moment. Is it correct that nothing will be done on the public building without recourse to the town planning commission? Would that be definite?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not know what progress has been made. Oh, yes; every representation that was made will be taken into account. But it is far more complicated than the hon. gentleman thinks to get this site in St. John's. Most of my troubles in public works have been in deciding on a site and in getting the local people to agree that
Supply-Public Works
it is the proper site. You two hon. members from St. John's do not, I think, agree.
We agree on the site; we agree where it should not be.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we shall continue with the estimates of the Department of Public Works, and then take up the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. On Friday we shall take up the Income Tax Act. We hope to have that concluded early enough tb deal with the resolution concerning the superannuation act. That resolution is the basis of a bill to amend the superannuatioh act. The bill will be referred to a committee, and we should like to see it sent to the committee as soon as possible.
